title: Every Spot Where All Words Line Up
statement:
You get a string text and a list words in which every word has the same length. Words may repeat in the list.

Find every index i where the slice of text starting at i is exactly all the words glued together in some order, each used exactly as many times as it appears in words, with nothing in between. Return those indexes in increasing order (an empty list if there are none).

examples.why: "abcd" at 1, "cdab" at 3 and "cdab" at 8. Matches may overlap, and 3 does not line up with the word boundaries of the match at 1.
"ab" must appear twice in each match: "abcdab", "cdabab" and "ababcd".
Each match uses four letters. Both windows of length 4 split into "aa" + "aa".

constraints: text and words contain only lowercase letters
hints: The answer window always has length (number of words) × (word length). Checking every start with a word counter works, but repeats a lot of work.
A match is made of whole words, so it lines up with every word-length step from its start. Split the starts by i mod wordLength; within one group, the text is just a sequence of words.

For each offset, slide a window over that word sequence with a count map. On an unknown word, reset. On a word that is now too frequent, drop words from the left until it is not. When the window holds exactly all words, record its start.

explain.intuition:
Let w be the word length and m the number of words. Checking each start means cutting m words and comparing counts, which is O(n · m · w) overall. The waste is that neighbouring starts i and i + w share almost all their words.

So group starts by i mod w. Within one group, read the text as a list of w-letter tokens and run the usual "window with a count map" over tokens, like finding an anagram, but with words as letters. Each token enters and leaves the window at most once per offset, so all w offsets together cost O(n · w) for the slicing. Results from different offsets interleave, so sort at the end.
steps: Count the words into need. Let w be the word length and m the number of words.
For each offset o from 0 to w − 1: set left = o, an empty have map and used = 0.
Step right from o by w. Take the token at right. If it is not in need, clear the window and move left past it.
Otherwise add it. While its count exceeds need, remove the token at left and move left by w. If used = m, record left, then drop the leftmost token so the window can move on.
Sort and return all recorded starts.
pitfalls: Only sliding by whole words from index 0. Matches can start at any offset, like 3 in the first example.
Comparing sets of words instead of counts. For ["ab", "ab", "cd"], the window "abcdcd" has the same set of words but the wrong counts.
Clearing the window on an over-used word instead of shrinking it from the left. That skips matches that start just after the old start.

solutions.title: Check every start
solutions.idea: For each start, cut the window into words and compare their counts with the needed counts, stopping at the first mismatch.

solutions.title: Sliding window per offset
solutions.idea: Split the starts by index mod word length. For each offset, slide a window of whole words with a count map.
solutions.py:
class Solution:
    def allWordsLineUp(self, text: str, words: List[str]) -> List[int]:
        w, m, n = len(words[0]), len(words), len(text)
        need = Counter(words)
        out = []
        for o in range(w):
            left, used = o, 0
            have = Counter()
            for right in range(o, n - w + 1, w):
                t = text[right:right + w]
                if t not in need:
                    have.clear()
                    used = 0
                    left = right + w
                    continue
                have[t] += 1
                used += 1
                while have[t] > need[t]:
                    have[text[left:left + w]] -= 1
                    used -= 1
                    left += w
                if used == m:
                    out.append(left)
                    have[text[left:left + w]] -= 1
                    used -= 1
                    left += w
        return sorted(out)

followups: The words may have different lengths. Which part of the fast solution breaks?
Instead of exact matches, allow at most one foreign word inside the window. How would you change the window rules?
